narration:
Cars are supposed to stay on the road, but Tesla just made one leave it.
And that one viral clip is mixing different machines and different tricks.
In the next few minutes, we'll go through how it drives, how it sticks to a wall upside down,
how the rocket version gets into the air, and whether any of this is a real car or just a show.
Let's start with the boring part, because that's where the whole thing begins.
The battery stores the energy, and the power electronics decide how much goes to the motors.
The motors turn the wheels, and the tires push against the road.
There's no petrol and no rocket in this part, it's a normal electric car doing what electric cars do.
Every crazy moment in that video starts with plain driving.
How does a car hold on when it's upside down?
That's the fans.
They suck the air out from under the car, and a seal around the bottom stops new air rushing back in.
The pressure under the car drops, and the normal air above pushes the whole car down onto the surface.
That presses the tires harder into the surface, so they grip more and the car can take corners faster.
That's how Tesla drove it up a curved wall and held it upside down with the fans running.
But understand this, the fans don't lift anything, they glue the car down.
Anyone calling that part flying is wrong, that's grip.
The part where it really goes into the air is a different car.
Tesla lists three versions, Performance, Thrust and Rocket, and each one has different hardware.
The Performance one keeps two seats and the fans.
The Rocket one has one seat and extra thrusters for lift and rotation.
Inside it, high pressure tanks feed what's called cold gas thrusters.
The gas shoots out of nozzles around the car one way, and the car gets pushed the other way.
That's Newton's third law, the same cold gas idea NASA uses for short moves in space.
But the tanks only hold so much gas, so the push only lasts a moment.
That moment is enough to lift it, flip it or roll it, and bring it back down on its wheels.
That one really does leave the ground, but it's a one seat prototype, not the car you'd drive to work.
Now, is this a real flying car or a show?
Tesla itself lists the Rocket model as not approved for public roads.
Independent reporting called the car at the event a one off demonstration.
And we've seen one good jump, nothing yet like repeated launches and landings that prove the fans, seals and tanks hold up.
Then there's everything a real car has to survive, a crash, a hard landing, noise, servicing and the extra weight.
So the driving is real, the grip is real, and the flying is a prototype.
Until Tesla shows repeat flights and gets it certified for safety, that's all it is.
The simple version is, motors move the car, fans keep it stuck down, and gas thrusters push one special version into the air for a moment.
The car left the road, but whether it ever becomes a flying car you can own is still decided on the ground.
And if you want the next big tech clip broken down like this, follow the channel.
So here's the question, should Tesla certify the Rocket Roadster, or keep it as a prototype?

research.summary:
Tesla’s demonstration combined three different ideas that should not be treated as one ordinary road car. The Roadster’s basic motion comes from its battery-powered electric motors: power electronics send electricity from the traction battery to the motors, which turn the wheels and propel the car on the ground. That is the conventional electric-vehicle part of the story. [Source: https://afdc.energy.gov/vehicles/how-do-all-electric-cars-work]

A second system uses electrically driven fans and a ground-sealing arrangement to pull air from beneath the car. The resulting pressure difference pushes the vehicle toward the surface, increasing tire load and therefore available grip. It is not a substitute for the motors and it does not make the car fly; it is an aerodynamic traction system. Tesla demonstrated the concept by driving a prototype up a curved structure and holding it upside down. Tesla says the system is intended to improve traction and high-speed cornering. [Source: https://www.caranddriver.com/news/a74165059/tesla-roadster-thrusters-fan-system-explained/]

The spectacular airborne maneuvers came from a separate, limited configuration. Tesla’s Rocket version uses high-pressure tanks and cold-gas thrusters. When compressed gas is expelled through nozzles, the reaction force pushes the car in the opposite direction. NASA describes cold-gas propulsion as a system in which compressed gas is expelled through a nozzle to generate thrust; it is useful for short, controlled maneuvers but has limited total impulse. In Tesla’s demonstration, the thrusters briefly pushed the car upward and forward and provided rotational control for a flip or barrel roll. [Sources: https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/4-in-space-propulsion-chapter-2026-final.pdf?emrc=6a22e4bcb0da2; https://www.caranddriver.com/news/a74145531/tesla-roadster-revealed/]

The distinction matters. Tesla has described Performance, Thrust, and Rocket configurations: Performance has two seats and the fan system; Thrust adds rear cold-gas thrusters; Rocket is a one-seat configuration with additional thrusters around the vehicle for upward and rotational movement. The flying demonstration therefore should be understood as a limited, specialized prototype—not evidence that a normal, fully certified passenger car can routinely fly on public roads. Tesla’s website says the Rocket model is not approved for public-road use, while the Associated Press reported that the event featured a one-off car and that production and regulatory approval remain unresolved. [Sources: https://www.tesla.com/roadster?redirect=no; https://www.caranddriver.com/news/a74145531/tesla-roadster-revealed/; https://apnews.com/article/tesla-musk-roadster-rocket-7d5f19665435b7408025bfb7a2f2f0b7]

The central practical question is not whether the stunt obeyed physics—it appears to have used real electric drive, fan-generated downforce, and compressed-gas thrust—but whether those systems can be made durable, affordable, crashworthy, quiet, serviceable, and compliant with vehicle regulations. In the United States, manufacturers must certify vehicles against applicable Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards before sale. Until Tesla publishes final specifications, demonstrates repeatable operation, and certifies a production version, the jump and flip are best treated as an engineering demonstration rather than a proven consumer-vehicle capability. [Sources: https://www.nhtsa.gov/laws-regulations; https://www.nhtsa.gov/document/mission-office-vehicle-safety-compliance-ovsc; https://apnews.com/article/tesla-musk-roadster-rocket-7d5f19665435b7408025bfb7a2f2f0b7]

Tesla’s new Roadster appears to drive up a wall, hold itself upside down, and briefly fly. But the viral footage combines several different systems and Roadster versions, so the details matter.

This video explains how the electric motors move the car, how fans create suction to increase grip, and how cold-gas thrusters lift and rotate the one-seat Rocket version. We also look at whether this is a real flying car or an impressive prototype that is not approved for public roads.
